what_its_for: Terazosin is used to treat two conditions: (1) High blood pressure (hypertension) — it helps relax your blood vessels so your heart does not have to work as hard. (2) Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) — an enlarged prostate in men. It relaxes the muscles in the prostate and bladder neck, making it easier to urinate.
how_to_take: Take terazosin by mouth, with or without food. It is very important to take your FIRST dose at bedtime to reduce the risk of dizziness or fainting. After that, you can take it at the same time each day, either in the morning or at night — whatever works best for you. Swallow the capsule whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time every day to keep a steady level in your body.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose (usually 1 mg at bedtime) and slowly increase it over several weeks based on how well it works and how you feel. The usual dose for high blood pressure or BPH is 1 mg to 10 mg once daily. Do not change your dose on your own — always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for the one you missed. If you have missed several doses in a row, call your doctor before restarting, as you may need to start again at a low dose to avoid dizziness.
storage: Store terazosin at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do NOT store it in the bathroom. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking terazosin — it can increase dizziness and lower your blood pressure too much. Avoid standing up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, especially in the first few hours after taking a dose, as this can cause dizziness or fainting (this is called orthostatic hypotension). Be careful when driving or using machinery until you know how this medication affects you. Avoid other medications that lower blood pressure unless your doctor says it is okay — this includes some cold medicines, erectile dysfunction drugs (like sildenafil/Viagra), and herbal supplements like saw palmetto.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden severe dizziness or fainting, a fast or irregular heartbeat, chest pain, shortness of breath, swelling of your hands, feet, or ankles, a painful erection that lasts more than 4 hours (priapism), or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also call your doctor if your blood pressure is not improving or your urinary symptoms are getting worse.
when_it_works: For high blood pressure, you may start to see an effect within a few hours of your first dose, but it may take several weeks of consistent use to get the full benefit. For enlarged prostate (BPH) symptoms such as difficulty urinating, it may take 2 to 4 weeks before you notice significant improvement. Keep taking your medication even if you feel well — do not stop without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults (65+): You are more sensitive to the blood pressure-lowering effects of this medication and have a higher risk of dizziness and falls. Take extra care when standing up, and consider using support (like holding onto furniture) to prevent falls. Pregnant women: Terazosin is generally not recommended during pregnancy. Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if terazosin passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have kidney or liver disease. Children: Terazosin is not typically used in children.
